newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Dec 11.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Dec 11.

text.p: THE DOMINION

NZ First leader Winston Peters has extracted a powerful new role as New Zealand's treasurer as part of the price of a coalition deal with National. Turning his back on his savage anti-National election campaign, Peters anointed his old enemy Jim Bolger on Tuesday night as the country's historic first MMP prime minister. National's Bill Birch is to stay on as finance minister, but his staff acknowledged on Tuesday night it would be as a junior minister. Peters's role as treasurer will be based on the Australian model, where the treasurer is responsible for overall economic policy, and delivers the
budget, and oversees macroeconomic policy. The finance minister is responsible for taxation and savings. Page 1.

Economc and political stability topped the list of reasons that NZ First leader Winston Peters offered on Tuesday night for forming a coalition with National. He emphasised political security and economic growth ahead of "judicious" spending on social policy. Peters reassured the financial markets that the coalition would be moderate in spending and economic policy, indicating that the fear that a Labour-NZ First deal would spook investors was a significant factor in the decision. Page 1.

Fighting back tears on Tuesday night, Helen Clark ruled out resigning from Labour's leadership despite losing the race for the Beehive. Clark, who missed out on becoming New Zealand's first female prime minister, may come under pressure from within the caucus after her failure. Clark learned of the NZ First decision from television news after NZ First president Doug Woollerton was delayed in getting a note to her. She said she believed Labour had lost out on a coalition deal because it had stuck to its principles and bottom lines. Labour was also not prepared to budge on dividing up the finance minister's job.
Page 1.

An explosion destroyed the government limousine of Prime Minister Jim Bolger outside his chauffeur's house early on Wednesday morning. Residents of Wellington's Karori suburb said a can of petrol had been thrown through the back window of the car, setting it on fire. Page 1.

NZ First's rejection 0f Labour as its coalition partner seems to have made the Alliance's heart grow fonder toward its failed colleagues on the left. Alliance leader Jim Anderton on Tuesday night pledged strong support for Labour and Labour leader Helen Clark. He said he expected to work closely with Labour in Opposition. Page 2.

National and NZ First's financial package will be vulnerable to floor-crossing by government MPs after ACT NZ said on Tuesday night it would not support much of the new government's economic policy. The support of ACT's 13 MPs could be crucial for the
coalition parliament, which holds just 61 of parliament's 120 seats. Page 2.

NZ First leader Winston Peters did not let his caucus know his own preference for a coalition partner till near the end of its nine-hour decision meeting, according to caucus secretary Deborah Morris. Te Tai Tonga MP Tu Wyllie, who said it took a lot to persuade him to support the deal with National, also denied that Peters had exerted much personal influence. Page 2.

The Apple and Pear Board has rejected Apple Field's application to independently export 1.5 million cartons of apples. Board chairman John McCliskie said on Tuesday the proposal was not in the interests of New Zealand's 1,600 growers and could actually diminish returns to New Zealand. Apple Fields managing director Tom Kain described the decision as a tragedy for the New Zealand apple industry. The company was locked in discussions with its lawyers and international partners, and would announce its future on Thursday afternoon, he said. Page 3.

Tranz Rail revenues are up, but by relatively small percentages because of the economic downturn, according to chairman Ed Burkhardt. Speaking after the company's first annual meeting in Wellington on Tuesday, Burkhardt said that with small increases in business and cost control "our bottom-line is getting better". "But we'd have a stronger performance if we saw better business conditions." Page 21.

The aborted cable services agreement between Telecom and Sky Television would have meant a close working relationship between the two. The agreement included provisions for Telecom to extend Sky's broadcast area at its own cost in exchange for revenue sharing, and joining in marketing, programming and other joint efforts with the pay television operator. Page 21.

Listed fishing company Sanford said on Tuesday it was trading satisfactorily despite "laughable" economic policies. Managing director David Anderson told shareholders at the company's annual meeting in Auckland that Sanford had made big
savings in a cost-cutting exercise but these paled into insignificance compared with the lossses in selling prices from the high dollar. Page 21.
THE NEW ZEALAND HERALD

National has handed its biggest foe, Winston Peters, the massive power of writing the next budget in a coalition pact which holds reasonably firm on economic policy, but flags more money for health, education and jobs. In his dramatic announcement live into the nation's homes on Tuesday night, the NZ First leader waited until the final paragraph of a lengthy statement before revealing National to be the "winner" of the eight weeks of coalition talks. As leader of the minor coalition partner, Peters becomes Deputy Prime Minister, but in the major and crucial concession Labour was unwilling to offer, the NZ

First leader will also take the new post of Tresurer. Peters has secured his cherished referendum on compulsory superannuation, widened inflation targets, deferred next year's tax cuts, won changes to the Employment Contracts Act and, it is understood, wiped the superannuation surcharge.

Countrywide Bank reacted instantly to the coalition announcement on Tuesday night by slashing its floating home mortgage rate to 9.95 percent from 10.75 percent. The bank's managing director David Wolfenden conceded that the move would not have been made if Labour had won NZ First's backing. He said

he had not realised Winston Peters had been made Treasurer when the decision was taken. Ord Minnett broker Arthur Lim said the announcement was a relief for the share market. The markets were further soothed when Reserve Bank governor Don Brash indicated on Tuesday night that he was happy with monetary policy changes announced by NZ First leader Peters. Brash visited the Beehive on Tuesday night to sign the changes to new policy target agreements with Finance Minister Bill Birch. The inflation target has been expanded to 0-3 percent from the former target of 0-2 percent.

Labour believes its refusal to carve up the finance role so that Winston Peters could have a piece of the action may have cost it the Beehive. And the New Zealand Herald understands that Tau Henare -- one of the strongest advocates for Labour among the NZ First MPs -- was still pursuing the issue with Labour late Tuesday afternoon. But Labour refused, saying iy was a "non negotiable item".

Fallout was swift within NZ First on Tuesday night with the first resignation logged immediately after the coalition choice and predictions of a serious popularity slump. Two-time candidate Patra de Coudray said she began writing her resignation on hearing the deciaion. "I did not campaign to support National."

Maori support for NZ First is likely to dive, says the head of the Waikato University research unit that polled Maori voters before and after the election. Grabriel Dekel said the five Maori MPs would also come under huge pressure from NZ First's

Maori supporters, who still had sympathies with Labour, to go independent. He said his polls showed support for a NZ First-National coalition only if the Prime MInister Jim Bolger were to go. "So I think Winston's made a huge mistake for the future of his party."

Business leaders greeted Tuesday night's coalition announcement with relief, but were cautious about predicting the long-term impact until the fiscal picture became clearer. "My reaction is that it is probably as good a result as could have been achieved under the cirucmstances," said managing director

of chemicals giant Fernz Corporation Kerry Hoggard. Cavill White Securities sharebroker Don Turkington said the coalition was the result markets had been looking for, and was the basis for a sustained rally in the share and bond markets.

National Mutual Holdings on Tuesday reported a higher-than-expected tax-paid profit of A$210.88 million (NZ$240.40 million) for the September 30 year, buoyed by a substantial turnaround in the performance of its life unit National Mutual Life.
